paper_title: Dream2Discern: Learning from Hard Latent Variants for Runtime Failure Prediction in Multi-Agent Systems

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reliable deployment of LLM-based multi-agent systems calls for runtime auditors that predict terminal outcomes from observed execution prefixes. These auditors typically learn from a limited corpus of trajectories with verified outcomes. Expanding this corpus requires costly execution and verification, yet broader failure coverage alone provides no explicit criterion for identifying prefixes that the current auditor finds difficult to classify. To this end, we propose Dream2Discern, a runtime auditor trained through implicit augmentation guided by its own prediction loss. During Dream, we select perturbations of the auditor's representation operators to increase prediction loss on recorded prefixes, yielding hard latent variants. During Discern, the auditor learns to predict execution outcomes from these variants using the original labels. The variants are regenerated as the auditor learns, turning a limited corpus into a renewable source of hard examples and requiring no additional trajectory collection or outcome verification. Extensive evaluations on AFTraj-2K and StepShield show that Dream2Discern outperforms competitive failure auditors and achieves over 90% trajectory-level weighted accuracy on both benchmarks while balancing prediction accuracy and timeliness. sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: LLM-based multi-agent systems coordinate specialized agents and tools to solve complex tasks, from software development to open-ended web interaction (Wu et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2023; Fourney et al., 2024). However, the complexity of these tasks and their execution environments makes agents prone to reasoning and tool-use errors that can potentially compromise task completion (Cemri et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025c). In open-world environments, these errors can lead agents to make unnecessary tool calls or modify external systems in unintended ways (Li et al., 2023b; Ruan et al., 2024; Oh et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025a). Accordingly, reliable deployment calls for runtime failure prediction, where an auditor assesses the risk of eventual task failure from the execution history observed so far to inform timely intervention (Zhang et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). Despite its importance, existing learning-based runtime auditors, such as TRACES (Li et al., 2026) and AgentForesight (Zhang et al., 2026), typically rely on limited corpus of carefully curated trajectories with verified outcomes, as illustrated in Figure 1(a). straightforward way to improve these auditors is to augment the training corpus to cover broader range of failure scenarios, either by collecting new trajectories or by editing existing ones (Figure 1(b)). However, collecting new trajectories requires agent rollouts and outcome verification, making corpus expansion costly to scale (Xie et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2025). Editing recorded trajectories reuses the observed history, but changing an action or tool response can alter the continuation and invalidate the original outcome Corresponding author 1 Research preprint Figure 1. Motivation of Dream2Discern. (a) runtime auditor predicts terminal outcomes from observed prefixes but learns from limited labeled corpus. (b) Trajectory augmentation seeks broader failure coverage, but collection is costly and editing can invalidate outcome labels (right). Broader coverage alone does not identify prefixes that the current auditor finds hard to classify. (c) We construct hard latent variants through operator perturbations chosen to increase batch prediction loss, then train on these variants while keeping recorded prefixes and labels unchanged. label, requiring resumed execution and re-verification (Kong et al., 2026; Bonagiri et al., 2026). More fundamentally, broader failure coverage alone provides no explicit criterion for identifying trajectories whose prefixes the current auditor finds difficult to assess. These considerations naturally motivate the following research question: RESEARCH QUESTION Can we identify and exploit the current auditors hard cases without acquiring additional labeled trajectories? To address this question, we propose an implicit augmentation approach that constructs hard latent variants within the auditor (Figure 1(c)). Our key insight is to use the auditors own prediction loss as criterion for deciding which variants to construct. We perturb the auditors representation computation to increase prediction loss on recorded prefixes, yielding hard latent variants for training with the original outcome labels. To realize this idea, we develop Dream2Discern, runtime auditor that alternates between two training steps: constructing hard latent variants (Dream) and learning from them to discern execution outcomes (Discern). Specifically, during Dream, we search for bounded, low-rank perturbations to the auditors query and value projection weights that increase batch prediction loss on recorded prefixes. We keep the prediction head fixed during this search, thus restricting the induced difficulty to changes in prefix representations. In Discern, we train the auditor to distinguish success from failure under the selected perturbation. At runtime, the trained auditor operates without perturbations, assigning failure score to each observed prefix and applying calibrated threshold to predict the terminal outcome. Together, the Dream and Discern steps alternate throughout training, allowing the constructed variants to evolve with the auditor. We conduct extensive runtime evaluations of Dream2Discern on AFTraj-2K (Zhang et al., 2026) and StepShield (Felicia et al., 2026). Our method achieves over 90% trajectory-level weighted accuracy (wACC) on both benchmarks and outperforms the strongest auditor baseline by up to 11.11% wACC, Research preprint while maintaining practical accuracytimeliness trade-off. These gains extend to Llama backbones, and loss-guided variants improve outcome discrimination over training without perturbations or with random perturbations. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: We show that augmenting the training corpus with edited prefixes does not improve held-out prediction under fixed training budget. This motivates constructing hard latent variants tailored to the current auditor (Section 3.1). We develop Dream2Discern, parameter-efficient runtime auditor with alternating Dream and Discern updates. Dream constructs hard latent variants through loss-guided perturbations of the auditors representation computation, and Discern learns to predict execution outcomes from these variants using the recorded labels (Section 3.2 and Section 3.3). We demonstrate improved prediction performance on AFTraj-2K and StepShield across different model families. Ablations and further analyses support the effectiveness of loss-guided variant construction and its contribution to runtime auditor learning (Section 4).

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: We present Dream2Discern, runtime auditor trained through alternating Dream and Discern steps. We first analyze the limitations of trajectory augmentation and motivate prediction loss as criterion for constructing hard latent variants. We then describe Dream, which constructs hard latent variants by perturbing the auditors adapted representation path. The Discern step trains the auditor under the selected perturbation. Finally, we describe how prefix failure scores yield runtime decisions. 3 Research preprint

sections.title: 3.1 Motivation
sections.content: Reliable deployment of LLM-based multi-agent systems calls for runtime failure prediction to support timely intervention. Existing learning-based auditors typically learn from limited corpus of carefully curated trajectories with verified outcomes. To improve prediction, straightforward approach is to augment this corpus to cover broader range of failure scenarios (Xu et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2026). However, the practical value of this approach depends on both the cost of acquiring additional labeled trajectories and whether they improve held-out prediction. To this end, we first assess the cost of acquiring additional labeled trajectories. We measure the combined rollout and outcome-verification time for 2K trajectories across task domains in AFTraj2K (Zhang et al., 2026) (see the right panel of Figure 1(b)). Results show that averaged acquisition times reach tens of seconds per trajectory, making repeated corpus expansion time-consuming and unsustainable. Editing offers an alternative by reusing recorded history, but the resulting continuation may no longer share the original outcome label. To examine this issue, we modify an action or tool response and resume execution, obtaining 326 verified continuations in AFTraj2K (see Appendix D.1.1 for detailed settings). Among verified continuations from failed source trajectories, 85.7% succeed, showing that source labels cannot simply be reused after editing and re-execution. Beyond acquisition cost, we examine whether the verified edits improve auditor learning. We first compare paired original and edited prefix representations extracted by the same frozen LLM encoder. Despite their textual differences, the two groups substantially overlap in shared PCA projection (Figure 2(a)). To evaluate their training utility, we train prediction heads on original prefixes alone (Original) or together with the verified edits (+Edited), keeping the encoder and optimization budget fixed. We evaluate both heads on the same held-out prefixes using class-balanced BCE, where lower loss indicates better prediction. The higher loss of +Edited relative to Original (Figure 2(b)) shows that these edits do not improve held-out prediction under this budget. These observations motivate us to construct hard latent variants that target the auditors prediction difficulties. We propose to seek bounded weight perturbations that alter prefix representations toward higher batch prediction loss, while preserving the recorded prefixes and outcome labels. To examine this intuition, we select perturbation using only training prefixes and temporarily apply it to the encoder, keeping the Original prediction head fixed. On the same held-out prefixes, the perturbed auditor (+Dream) has higher BCE than Original (Figure 2(b)). This result shows that the loss-guided perturbation also makes outcome prediction harder beyond the batch used to select it, without acquiring additional labeled trajectories. sections.content: Benchmarks. We evaluate runtime auditing on AFTraj-2K (Zhang et al., 2026) and StepShield (Felicia et al., 2026). AFTraj-2K contains multi-agent executions spanning mathematical reasoning, coding, and tool use, while StepShield provides annotated agent trajectories for safety monitoring. We train Dream2Discern separately for each benchmark and evaluate it on the corresponding test partition. The test split of AFTraj-2K comes from the same corpus as the training split and provides in-domain evaluation, whereas the test trajectories of StepShield come from incident templates never used in training and provide out-of-domain evaluation at the template level. sections.title: 4.4 Mechanism Analysis
sections.content: We analyze how Dream constructs hard latent variants and how sensitivity to its perturbations relates to held-out prediction errors. Appendix D.2 provides detailed experimental settings and analyses. Variant construction. We first examine whether Dream constructs harder latent variants than random perturbations do. After training Qwen3-8B with Dream2Discern, we fix its learned parameters and sample 50 batches of 32 prefixes from the AFTraj-2K training set. For each batch, we construct loss-guided Dream perturbation and sample random perturbations using the same settings. We temporarily apply each candidate and measure the change in batch BCE relative to the unperturbed auditor on the same prefixes. Each point in Figure 5a summarizes one batch, using the median of two draws for random perturbations. Dream increases loss on every batch, whereas random changes cluster near zero. This contrast shows that loss-guided search finds representation changes that make outcome prediction harder for the fixed auditor. Dream sensitivity. We next examine whether perturbations selected on training batches are informative about the auditors prediction errors on held-out prefixes. We use fixed Qwen3-4B auditor trained without perturbations and construct eight Dream perturbations from separate training batches. For each held-out AFTraj-2K prefix, we measure the absolute change in its failure score under each perturbation and average these changes to obtain its Dream sensitivity. We sort prefixes by sensitivity into five equal-sized groups and compute each groups error rate from the unperturbed predictions and recorded outcomes. Figure 5b shows that error rates increase from the lowest to the highest sensitivity group. This association suggests that loss-guided perturbations reflect weaknesses in the auditors learned outcome discrimination, supporting the construction of hard latent variants around prediction difficulties that also arise on held-out prefixes.

sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: LLM-based agentic systems. LLM-based agents combine reasoning, actions, and tool use to interact with external environments (Yao et al., 2022; Schick et al., 2023; Zhang and Zhang, 2025). Frameworks such as AutoGen (Wu et al., 2024), MetaGPT (Hong et al., 2023), and CAMEL (Li et al., 2023a) organize these capabilities through specialized roles and inter-agent communication. GPTSwarm (Zhuge et al., 2024) further optimizes prompts and agent connectivity, while MagenticOne (Fourney et al., 2024) coordinates web browsing, file navigation, and code execution. Other work studies how agents retain information across interactions (Sun et al., 2026b) and how their reliability changes over deployed lifespan (Zhu et al., 2026). Alongside these advances, reliable deployment requires assessing whether an ongoing execution is likely to fail, motivating our focus on runtime prediction from observed prefixes. Failure analysis for LLM agents. Failure analysis characterizes errors in agent executions and provides guidance for diagnosis and improvement. Common interface corruptions can also disrupt computer-use agents without adversarial intent (Sun et al., 2026a). MAST (Cemri et al., 2026) organizes multi-agent failures around system design, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification. Who&When (Zhang et al., 2025c) benchmarks attribution to responsible agents and decisive error steps, while AgenTracer (Zhang et al., 2025b) uses counterfactual replay and fault injection to construct supervision for trained failure tracer. AgentDebug (Zhu et al., 2025) diagnoses errors across agent components and generates corrective feedback to support recovery. OAT (Yeh et al., 2026) learns trajectory dynamics from successful executions and uses deviations from these dynamics to locate error steps in failed trajectories. Extending attribution beyond failed executions, Qian et al. (2026) study which historical interactions and evidence drive an agents actions. These studies support diagnosis and improvement, while runtime prediction complements them by assessing terminal outcomes before execution finishes, when intervention remains possible. Runtime failure prediction. Runtime auditors estimate outcomes from partial execution histories to support timely decisions. For vision-language-action policies, SAFE (Gu et al., 2026) predicts failure from internal features, while Hide-and-Seek (Park et al., 2026) discovers temporally structured failure signals through contrastive learning with trajectory-level labels. For LLM agents, AgentForesight (Zhang et al., 2026) trains an online auditor with decisive-error annotations, whereas TRACES (Li et al., 2026) models the temporal evolution of latent risk features from trajectory-level supervision. PrefixGuard (Huang et al., 2026) learns prefix-risk monitors from structured trace representations, and Baidya et al. (2026) combine sparse failure evidence with learned stopping policy. Related safety guardrails include AgentDoG (Liu et al., 2026), which provides contextual risk diagnosis for agent trajectories. StepGuard (Zheng et al., 2026) combines context-matched safe and unsafe trajectories with reinforcement learning that balances performance across these classes to assess tool actions before execution. We focus on the complementary question of how to target the auditors current prediction difficulties without expanding its trajectory corpus. Dream2Discern uses its prediction loss to construct hard latent variants of recorded prefixes and learns from them with the original outcome labels, without additional trajectory collection or verification. 11 Research preprint

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: In this paper, we highlight that broader failure coverage alone does not identify the current auditors hard cases, motivating implicit augmentation guided by prediction loss. To realize this idea, we present Dream2Discern, runtime auditor that learns from hard latent variants without acquiring additional labeled trajectories. Dream constructs these variants through loss-guided operator perturbations, and Discern learns from them using the original outcome labels. The learned auditor operates without perturbations at runtime. Evaluations on AFTraj-2K and StepShield across model families demonstrate improved runtime failure prediction. These findings support targeting the auditors current prediction difficulties to improve learning from fixed trajectory corpus. 12 Research preprint

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: This work studies runtime failure prediction on existing agent-trajectory benchmarks to support reliable agent deployment. Auditor predictions can be incorrect and do not certify safe execution or prevent harmful actions. Deployment should retain task-specific safeguards and human oversight, and protect sensitive information in the execution histories supplied to the auditor.

For StepShield (Felicia et al., 2026), we use the paired clean/rogue trajectory subset in our evaluation corpus, with policy violations (failure) mapped to 𝑌𝑖 = 1 and clean (success) trajectories to 𝑌𝑖 = 0. For failed trajectory 𝑖, eligible prefixes end at 𝑡 = 𝐾𝑖, . . . , 𝑇𝑖, where 𝐾𝑖 is its annotated decisive step. We subsample equal numbers of success and failure prefixes within each combination of ending step, offset from the selected start, and terminal status. sections.title: D Supplementary Experimental Analyses
sections.content: D.1 Motivation Diagnostics We detail the trajectory-editing, representation, and learning diagnostics in Section 3.1. D.1.1 Trajectory Editing and Outcome Re-verification We select 128 mathematical reasoning and coding trajectories from the training pool of AFTraj-2K and make four edit attempts at one nonterminal action per source. GPT-5.4-mini editor uses the public task and observed history to propose an alternative action for the same agent, preserving the action type and tool schema without access to future interactions, outcome labels, or auditor feedback. After replaying preceding actions and matching their observations to the recorded history, we apply the edit and resume execution with GPT-5.4-mini under 40-message limit covering replay and continuation. Coding outcomes are determined by running the last program submitted by CodeWriter against the source tasks tests; these tests are not included in the continuation agents system prompts. Mathematical outcomes are checked against reference answers with LLM-assisted semantic review. We retain 326 verified continuations from 97 sources with valid execution histories and resolved labels under consistent outcome checks. We compare each continuations outcome with its verified source label to assess label reuse after editing and re-execution. D.1.2 Representation and Learning Diagnostics For Figure 2, we use frozen Qwen3-4B encoder and the verified edits described in Appendix D.1.1. Panel (a) projects 97 originaledited prefix pairs onto jointly fitted principal components; density contours use all 326 edits with equal total weight per source trajectory. For panel (b), we train two-layer MLP prediction heads on original prefixes alone (Original) or the combined original and 23 Research preprint edited pool (+Edited), using the same initialization and 1,000 AdamW updates with batch size 128 and learning rate 103. We expand the original training trajectories into all their prefixes and add prefixes from the verified continuations only in the +Edited condition. Feature standardization and class weights are computed from the original training pool and shared by both conditions. The plotted heads use seed 0. With the Original head fixed, we temporarily perturb the encoders query and value projections (+Dream), using per-projection rank cap 8 and relative radius 3 104; the perturbation is selected on balanced batch of 32 original training prefixes. All conditions are evaluated on the same 2,820 held-out prefixes after excluding source groups represented in training, using the mean of the success-class and failure-class BCE losses. The loss plane varies the head parameters along the difference between the two trained heads and scales the selected encoder perturbation independently. The displayed coordinates are 𝑥 = 𝑣(𝐿𝐷 𝐿𝑂) and 𝑦 = 𝑢(𝐿𝐸 𝐿𝑂), where 𝑢 interpolates the head parameters, 𝑣 scales the perturbation, and 𝐿𝑂, 𝐿𝐸, 𝐿𝐷 denote the three labeled losses. Under the fixed training budget, adding the verified edits does not reduce held-out prediction loss. The training-selected Dream perturbation increases loss on the same held-out prefixes with the Original head fixed, supporting hard latent variant construction beyond the search batch. D.2 Mechanism Analysis Both experiments use AFTraj-2K with fixed seed-0 auditors, without updating their parameters during measurement. The loss comparison uses the final Qwen3-8B trained with Dream2Discern, whereas the sensitivity analysis uses the final Qwen3-4B trained without perturbations. D.2.1 Variant Construction Setup. We sample 50 batches of 32 prefixes from the 8,454 entries in the training-prefix index described in Appendix C.2. Using sampling seed 0, we draw with replacement uniformly over parent groups, trajectories within each group, and indexed prefixes within each trajectory. sections.title: E Limitations
sections.content: Our evaluation focuses on textual execution histories and binary terminal outcomes. Extending the auditor to visual observations or finer-grained outcome categories remains future work. We assess prediction quality on recorded trajectories, with downstream intervention left to the deployment system. Evaluating how auditor-guided replanning, tool restrictions, or human assistance affects task success and execution cost requires closed-loop experiments.
